title: Kookaburras and kingfishers

names.gloss: small brownish kingfisher; when it sings, company is coming

identification.basis: The dictionary names the kookaburra, the 'bronze wing kookaburra', the azure and forest kingfishers, a white-tailed kingfisher and the small brown kingfisher whose song means visitors. Within 30 km of Karma Waters the Atlas records the blue-winged and laughing kookaburras and the forest, azure, sacred and red-backed kingfishers.

summary: **[wakuka](word:wakuka)** is the kookaburra and **[kururrungka](word:kururrungka)** the 'bronze wing kookaburra', the blue-winged kookaburra of the north; **[milman](word:milman)** the azure kingfisher of the river, **[yindili](word:yindili)** the forest kingfisher of the woodland, **[jiwal-jiwal](word:jiwal-jiwal)** a 'kingfisher, white tailed', and **[dabuy](word:dabuy)** a 'small brownish kingfisher', of which the dictionary says 'when this bird starts singing you know you will get company, that someone is travelling' [ref:hershberger1982]. The kookaburras are the woodland's snake-and-lizard hawks, waiting 'perched on a branch until it sees an animal on the ground and then flies down and pounces on its prey', 'lizards, insects, worms, snakes, mice'; the forest kingfisher does the same on a smaller scale, 'bugs, beetles, grasshoppers ... small fish, frogs and tadpoles, lizards, and snakes'; and the azure kingfisher on its low branch over the pool means fish and shrimps in the shallows under it [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra] [ref:wiki-forest-kingfisher] [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher]. The laughing kookaburra digs its nest into a termite nest in a tree, the red-backed kingfisher into a creek bank [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra] [ref:wiki-red-backed-kingfisher].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[wakuka](word:wakuka)** 'kookaburra' (the same word is also glossed 'species of crow'). **[kururrungka](word:kururrungka)** 'bronze wing kookaburra', which can only be the blue-winged kookaburra, the north's kookaburra with blue in the wing [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:wiki-bwk]. **[milman](word:milman)** 'azure kingfisher'. **[yindili](word:yindili)** 'forest kingfisher'. **[jiwal-jiwal](word:jiwal-jiwal)** 'kingfisher, white tailed'. **[dabuy](word:dabuy)** 'small brownish kingfisher ... When this bird starts singing you know you will get company, that someone is travelling', and in another entry 'spirit' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The kookaburras and kingfishers
sections.body:
**Blue-winged kookaburra** (*Dacelo leachii*, *kururrungka*). 'A large species of kingfisher native to northern Australia and southern New Guinea. Measuring around 40 cm, it is slightly smaller than the more familiar laughing kookaburra. It has cream-coloured upper- and underparts barred with brownish markings. It has blue wings and brown shoulders and blue rump. It is sexually dimorphic, with a blue tail in the male', a barred rufous tail in the female, and 'striking white eyes'; 'their call has been described as a maniacal cackling or barking' [ref:wiki-bwk]. The [woodland](entry:woodland) page has its diet by season: more insects, lizards and frogs in the wet, more crayfish and scorpions in the dry; and its enemies, the red goshawk, the rufous owl, and at the nest pythons, quolls and goannas [ref:wiki-bwk].

**Laughing kookaburra** (*Dacelo novaeguineae*, *wakuka*). 'A large kingfisher with a whitish head and a brown eye-stripe. The upperparts are mostly dark brown but there is a mottled light-blue patch on the wing'; 'a predator of a wide variety of small animals, the laughing kookaburra typically waits perched on a branch until it sees an animal on the ground and then flies down and pounces on its prey. Its diet includes lizards, insects, worms, snakes, mice'; it makes 'a hollow for a nest in an arboreal termite nest' [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra].

**Forest kingfisher** (*Todiramphus macleayii*, *yindili*). 'Predominantly a blue and white bird', '21.5–25.5 cm in length', 'blue wings, head and tail with white breast, abdomen and nape ... a black band stretching from the bill, through the eyes to the ear coverts'. 'The forest kingfisher hunts invertebrates, such as bugs, beetles, grasshoppers, spiders, dragonflies, cicadas, ants, adult and larval butterflies, and worms, as well as small fish, frogs and tadpoles, lizards, and snakes. The forest kingfisher watches from a high perch, dives to the ground or water to seize its prey (sally-pouncing), then returns directly to the perch' [ref:wiki-forest-kingfisher].

**Sacred kingfisher** (*T. sanctus*), 'a medium-sized woodland kingfisher that inhabits mangroves, woodlands, forests and river valleys', 'mostly blue-green to turquoise above with white underparts and collar feathers, a black mask and buff lores' [ref:wiki-sacred-kingfisher]. **Red-backed kingfisher** (*T. pyrrhopygius*), 'a predominantly blue-green and white bird with a chestnut rump', 20–24 cm; 'the call is a descending, mournful whistle "kee-ip", repeated every few seconds in a long series from a tree-top'; 'the breeding season is August to February ... although birds may not breed in times of drought. The nest is a burrow 0.5–1.25 m into the top third section of a steep sloping bank overlooking a dry creek-bed or dam' [ref:wiki-red-backed-kingfisher].

**Azure kingfisher** (*Ceyx azureus*, *milman*): the small deep-blue and orange kingfisher of the river's low branches, which dives for small fish and shrimps and nests in a tunnel in the bank; the [waterhole](entry:waterhole) page reads it as a sign of what is in the shallows below its perch [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher].

sections.heading: Telling them
sections.body:
- **Blue-winged kookaburra**: pale head with streaks, white eye, blue wings, no dark eye-stripe; a bark and cackle [ref:wiki-bwk].
- **Laughing kookaburra**: brown eye-stripe, dark eye, only a patch of blue on the wing; the laugh [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra].
- **Forest kingfisher**: blue and white with a black mask and a white spot before the eye, on a high perch in the woodland [ref:wiki-forest-kingfisher].
- **Sacred kingfisher**: greener, buff below, a buff spot before the eye [ref:wiki-sacred-kingfisher].
- **Red-backed kingfisher**: a chestnut rump and a streaked crown, on a dead tree-top over dry country, whistling [ref:wiki-red-backed-kingfisher].
- **Azure kingfisher**: tiny, deep blue above and orange below, on a stick a hand above the water [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher].
- **[Rainbow bee-eater](entry:bush-birds)**: also a bright, perching, sallying bird over the river, but green and gold with a long tail wire [ref:wiki-bee-eater].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **The laugh at dawn and dusk** marks the kookaburra family's territory [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra].
- **A hole dug into a termite nest on a tree trunk**: a kookaburra's nest [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra].
- **A burrow high in a creek bank** over a dry bed: the red-backed kingfisher [ref:wiki-red-backed-kingfisher].
- **An azure kingfisher on a low branch**: fish and shrimps in the shallows beneath [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher].
- **Crayfish and prawn shells under a perch**; see [waterhole](entry:waterhole) [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher].
- **The small brown kingfisher singing**: company coming, the dictionary says [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Where they live
sections.body: The kookaburras and the forest and sacred kingfishers in the [woodland](entry:woodland) and the river trees, on high perches over open ground; the red-backed kingfisher in the driest country with a bank to burrow in; the azure kingfisher only over the water [ref:wiki-bwk] [ref:wiki-forest-kingfisher] [ref:wiki-red-backed-kingfisher] [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher].

sections.heading: The watchers on the branch
sections.body: The kookaburras and kingfishers hunt by sitting still and dropping: a [snake](entry:snakes), a skink, a mouse, a grasshopper, a frog, a prawn, each taken from a perch and beaten on the branch [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra] [ref:wiki-forest-kingfisher]. The kookaburra is the one bird that eats the small [snakes](entry:snakes) in numbers, and the cane toad is now a hazard to it as to the goannas [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra] [ref:wiki-cane-toads]. Their nests in the termite nests and the banks are raided by the [pythons](entry:pythons), the [goannas](entry:goanna) and the quoll, and the birds themselves by the goshawk and the owls [ref:wiki-bwk]. Their calls are the woodland's clock: the laugh at first light and last, and the red-backed kingfisher's whistle through the heat of a dry-season day [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra] [ref:wiki-red-backed-kingfisher].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Kookaburras nest from September; the red-backed kingfisher from August to February 'often with a double brood', and not at all in a drought; the blue-winged kookaburra's diet turns from the wet's frogs and lizards to the dry's crayfish and scorpions [ref:wiki-bwk] [ref:wiki-red-backed-kingfisher]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **A sign of visitors**: the small brown kingfisher's song [ref:hershberger1982].
- **A sign of fish**: the azure kingfisher's perch [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher].
- **A clock and a sentry**: the kookaburra's laugh at the ends of the day and its scolding of a snake [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra].
- **Snake control** round the camp: a resident kookaburra family [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra].

sections.heading: Reading the kookaburras
sections.body:
1. **A kookaburra or a butcherbird scolding one spot** on the ground is a snake or a goanna; look before you walk there [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra].
2. **Follow the azure kingfisher** to the shallows with bait in them [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher].
3. **When the small brown kingfisher sings**, put the billy on; someone is coming [ref:hershberger1982].
4. **Leave the termite-nest hollows** on the trunks; they are nests [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra].
5. The kookaburras were not a hunted bird in any of the sources used here; the small birds of the east coast were taken as eggs and fledglings rather than adults [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Native birds are protected wildlife in Queensland under the *Nature Conservation Act 1992*; native title holders hunting for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs are covered by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* [ref:qld-nca] [ref:alrc].
- A kookaburra at the camp table will take meat from a plate and a finger with it.
- A bird scolding on the ground is a snake warning; see [snakes](entry:snakes) [ref:healthdirect-snakebite].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The dictionary's six names are a field guide waiting for speakers to say which bird is which [ref:hershberger1982]. The contribution box below is for that. Native title holders' rights differ from place to place: see each place above.

locations.summary: Kookaburras and kingfishers are everywhere on the Hann. The Atlas of Living Australia holds 3,395 records of them (1976–2026) in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru, most of them the **blue-winged kookaburra** (1,294) and the **laughing kookaburra** (1,017): both kookaburras live here together [ref:ala-hann-kingfishers]. Along the Hann the country is 'stringybark, bloodwood, Moreton Bay ash and ironbark' woodland [ref:wp-hann], their kind of country.

sections.heading: Which ones live here
sections.body: After the two kookaburras come the **forest kingfisher** (675 records), the **sacred kingfisher** (215), the **azure kingfisher** of the river (151) and the **red-backed kingfisher** of the dry country (34). The **little kingfisher** (4 records, 2003–2023), the **buff-breasted paradise-kingfisher** (2, 1990) and single yellow-billed and collared kingfishers have also been logged [ref:ala-hann-kingfishers]. The box takes in far more country than the Hann, so read the counts as 'lives in this country', not as a map.

sections.heading: Their year here
sections.body: The Hann never stops running, so its holes keep fish and shrimps through the late dry [ref:bom-105001b], and the azure kingfisher keeps to them. In the wet (December to March) the plains flood and food is everywhere [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture], the season when the blue-winged kookaburra eats more frogs and lizards (see above). By October 'the land is brown and parched' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]: the dry-country birds' time.

sections.heading: People and these birds here
sections.body: No published Possum, Thaypan, Kuku Warra or Lama Lama record describes using or hunting kookaburras or kingfishers. The Kuku Thaypan names below show they are known birds of this country; what they mean in story or law is for the Traditional Owners to tell.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: In Kuku Thaypan (Awu Alaya), the language of the Thaypan people of the middle and lower Hann, the blue-winged kookaburra is **arrolmba**, possibly a word shared with Olkola [ref:hgdb], and the sacred kingfisher **arodha** [ref:hgdb-sacred].

locations.summary: Both kookaburras are at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters), the blue-winged with thirty-three records and the laughing with twenty-seven, and four kingfishers with them: the forest, nineteen, the azure, eleven, the sacred, eight, and the red-backed, nine [ref:ala-aves].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: Both kookaburras laugh at Karma Waters, and the forest kingfisher is on every second dead branch in the dry; the dictionary's six names are a field guide waiting for the Western Yalanji to say which is which [ref:ala-aves] [ref:hershberger1982]. Here the native title rights that section 211 protects (see Safety above) are those recognised in the Western Yalanji determinations [ref:wyac2020].
